accroche: The white marble of antiquity owes much to lost color: statues were typically painted.
contenu_vulgarise:
When we think of Greek art, we picture white marble: smooth bodies without a trace of color. That image comes from museums, and it is wrong on one specific point. Greek and Roman statues were, typically, painted.

The Getty Museum says so plainly about its exhibition *The Color of Life* (2008): in antiquity, statues were typically painted. The evidence comes from several directions: wall paintings and vases that depict colored statues, Greek and Latin texts that mention painting figures, and laboratory analyses that find traces of the original color.

## Where Did the Color Go?

Pigments did not simply evaporate all at once. The Getty cites three causes: burial conditions, aging, and overly aggressive cleaning. The white we see therefore comes down to this loss: over time and through cleaning, the stone lost the paint that covered it.

A specific example: on a Greek terracotta *Head of a God* from about 325 BCE, Getty conservators identified Egyptian blue on the beard, reddish brown on the hair, and pink on the lips and face. A blue beard looks strange today. That is precisely what the object reveals.

## Reconstructing Without Pretending to Know

For more than 40 years, Vinzenz Brinkmann and Ulrike Koch-Brinkmann, at the Liebieghaus in Frankfurt, have been producing color reconstructions of marble and bronze statues, based on scientific research. The exhibition *Gods in Color* is presented in Munich from December 2003 to February 2004, then other cities host it: the Getty Villa in 2008, in the exhibition *The Color of Life*, and Frankfurt the same year; the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York takes part in 2022-2023, in the exhibition *Chroma*.

These reconstructions are hypotheses, and the list of reconstructed works shows it: the Peplos Kore exists in three variants. What the traces allow us to state is that the statue was painted; what they do not always settle is the arrangement of the colors. Not all statues were colored in the same way, moreover: the paint was often limited to clothing and hair, the skin remaining the color of the stone, but many of them were painted entirely.

repere.texte: Around 325 BCE: on a Greek terracotta Head of a God held at the Getty, conservators identified Egyptian blue on the beard, reddish brown on the hair, and pink on the lips and face.
repere.source: J. Paul Getty Museum, The Color of Life: Polychromy in Sculpture from Antiquity to the Present (2008)

carte.punch: Ancient statues were typically painted: the white owes much to lost color.
carte.idee: In antiquity, statues were typically painted. The color was lost through burial, aging, and overly aggressive cleaning. On a Greek terracotta head from about 325 BCE, the Getty found Egyptian blue on the beard.

quiz.question: Why do ancient statues almost always reach us without their colors?
choix: The paint disappeared through burial, time, and overly aggressive cleaning
The Greeks painted only bronze statues, never marble ones
The colors found are additions by modern restorers, not original pigments
Greek sculptors judged color unworthy of the image of a god
quiz.explication: The Getty attributes the loss of color to burial, aging, and overly aggressive cleaning. The wall paintings, vases, and Greek and Latin texts that mention painting figures show that the color was intended, and laboratory analyses find traces of ancient polychromy, which makes the idea of colors added after the fact unlikely. Marble statues also bore pigments, according to Wikipedia (Polychromy), so color was not limited to bronze.

quiz_supplementaire.question: For how long have Vinzenz Brinkmann and Ulrike Koch-Brinkmann been studying the polychromy of ancient sculptures, according to the entry?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Vinzenz Brinkmann and Ulrike Koch-Brinkmann, at the Liebieghaus in Frankfurt, have been studying polychromy for more than 40 years. Thirty years, about twenty years, or less than ten years are therefore contradicted by the text.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the entry, what do the traces of color on statues allow us to state, and what do they not always settle?
choix: The arrangement of the colors, but not the fact that the statue was painted
That all statues were painted in the same way
That the statue was painted, but not always the arrangement of the colors
That the skin was painted, but not the clothing
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The traces establish that the statue was painted. The reconstructions remain hypotheses about the arrangement of the colors, which the traces do not always settle. Not all statues were colored in the same way.
